prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: My own first choice in the opening round was B057, the experimental Higgs discovery, and I still regard it as the plainest discovery on the list. But the discussion has to start from what the eight ballots actually show, and B042 is the only candidate that every member ranked (three first places, two second places, my own third). It is also the case where the committee's central question, who is the person behind the discovery, has a clean answer. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme that removes the light shift and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group took strontium lattice clocks to the 1e-18 level and used them for relativistic redshift tests over millimetre scales and for constraints on fundamental constants. The result has been reproduced by several independent laboratories, clock comparisons now run over fibre links and across continents, and the work feeds directly into the discussion of redefining the second. It is original, experimentally verifiable and mature, which is the profile of a prize that can be given without apology. A two-laureate prize is also a perfectly acceptable configuration and avoids the arbitrary three-name cut that afflicts several other candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition: the 2005 prize (frequency-comb spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of single trapped ions, which underlies the ion-clock lineage) cover neighbouring ground, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 territory, so some will say the lattice clock is an application of a recognised toolbox rather than a new discovery. A second worry is that other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others) are outside the two credited names, and I cannot verify the priority history in detail. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and a committee that likes to see consequences realised might prefer to wait. Against B057 itself, my reservation is attribution: giving the prize to the three founding leaders honours instrument and project leadership, not the discovery-day analyses, and I should not let my enthusiasm for the physics hide that this is a policy choice about collaborations rather than a clean attribution.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B042 first on clarity and impact, and ranked B057 only fourth, arguing that crediting Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee recognises the founding of the detectors rather than the discovery analysis, and that the statutes are awkward for collaborations.
responses.response: I largely agree, and it is the main reason I am moving my preferred configuration away from my own first-ranked B057. In my opening ballot I called the leadership credit defensible but not the same as discovery credit, and Pearce states the same problem more sharply. Where I still differ is that I do not think the awkwardness makes B057 unprizable: the 2013 prize left the experimental half unrecognised, and the committee will sooner or later have to decide whether founders of the detectors are an acceptable proxy. I would keep B057 as a live alternative for that reason, but the clean attribution of B042 makes it the better configuration to present first.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B042 first because the magic-wavelength idea is simple and original, the laser-spectroscopy control is the core of it, and the 1e-18 performance has been confirmed by many laboratories, with the 2005 comb prize noted as the only overlap.
responses.response: I accept the scientific case and defer to Kroll on the laser-spectroscopy details, since that is his field and not mine. I would qualify the dismissal of the 2005 overlap: Ye's contribution is partly built on comb and ultrastable-laser technology, so the citation should be anchored on the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, not on generic precision spectroscopy. That keeps the prize separable from Hall and Hänsch, and I have worded the proposed citation accordingly.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B042 only sixth, citing overlap with the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes, that the redefinition of the SI second is still pending, and that other contributors complicate sharp attribution.
responses.response: This is the most serious disagreement with B042 and I do not think it can be waved away. My answer is that overlap with a prize for a tool is different from overlap with the discovery: the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured comb spectroscopy and single-ion control, and the lattice clock's distinctive step, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, was not part of either. On timing, I think the science is already confirmed independently, so waiting for a metrological decision by another body is not necessary. I do concede that Eriksson's point about other contributors is real and unresolved, and I would not claim the two-name attribution is airtight.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B038 (trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum computing foundations) first and B049 (circuit QED) second, and ranked B042 seventh, while noting overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that Ye appears in other groupings.
responses.response: I take the point that quantum-information platforms have larger industrial reach than clocks, but I do not think reach should substitute for scientific distinctness. B038 bundles ion computing foundations with cold-atom simulation and has the 2012 overlap that Johansson himself flags, and B049 sits right after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits, as Johansson also says. By his own account these are the candidates where timing and attribution are least settled, whereas B042 has neither problem to the same degree. I therefore see his own caveats as an argument for placing B042 ahead of B038 and B049 in this round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as an application of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control toolkits.

Whether other lattice-clock pioneers (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto) have a priority claim that the two-name credit cannot accommodate; I cannot verify this in detail from the supplied material.
Whether the committee will accept leadership of the ATLAS and CMS collaborations as the basis for B057, which determines how strong that alternative is.
Whether waiting for the formal redefinition of the second would be preferred by colleagues, and whether that should matter for a scientific prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B042 or for the alternatives. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and cosmology and do not involve any credited name on the shortlist. I am a theorist and not an expert in atomic clocks or collider detectors, so I rely on Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce for detail on the metrology.
